introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0560), Paper 2 - Modern World History Since 1870, ORDINARY LEVEL, JUNE 2023. Duration: Two and a Half Hours.**

Instructions to candidates:

- Answer FOUR Questions.
- TWO questions must be chosen from SECTION A, ONE from SECTION B and ONE other from SECTION C. One of the two questions chosen from SECTION A must be a Starred question.
- Maps should be used to illustrate answers where appropriate. All questions carry equal marks.

SECTION A: question 1 is compulsory in the sense that the candidate answers either 1A* or 1B* (the two Starred questions) and one other question from the section (2, 3 or 4). SECTION B: answer ONE question (5, 6 or 7). SECTION C: answer ONE question (8, 9 or 10).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION A: CAMEROON SINCE 1850**

Question one is compulsory. Answer either 1A* or 1B* and one other Question from this section.

**1. Or**

**B\* (Starred question)** Study this extract revolving around the organisation of a UN-supervised elections in British Cameroons in the 1960s and the political developments that followed and then answer questions (a) to (e) which follow. (The maximum mark for each sub question is indicated in brackets)

> The UN-supervised plebiscites of the early 1960s offered a unique opportunity for the people of British Cameroons to determine their political destiny. On the plebiscite day, tens of thousands of Southern Cameroonians showed up at the various polling stations to cast their votes. The electorate were expected to choose between two questions imposed by the UNO. The plebiscites revealed some interesting results. [line 5]
>
> While the electorate in Northern Cameroons voted in favour of the Nigerian proposition, their brothers and sisters in Southern Cameroons voted in favour of the Cameroon proposition. In Southern Cameroons, plans were underway to work out a framework for a possible union with the independent Republic of Cameroon. This framework would be validated in the constitution for the new Cameroon that was to be drafted in Foumban. Before their arrival in Foumban, the leaders of the Republic of Cameroon and Southern Cameroon held talks in Buea, Bamenda and Yaounde to discuss the idea of a possible union. The Foumban Conference that was held from the 17th to 21st July .... agreed on the main provisions of the constitution. [line 10]
>
> The Constitution put in place three governments, four Houses, a common currency ... The Republic of Cameroon and Southern Cameroons were respectively renamed the Federated State of East Cameroon [line 15] with headquarters in Yaounde and the Federated State of West Cameroon with headquarters in Buea. The two federated states would be autonomous entities placed under the administration of Prime Ministers appointed by the President of Republic. The Constitution was subsequently revisited several times and amended - a source of concern, suspicion and tension with long term consequences for the country.

*Source: Improvised text by members of the Subject Panel.*

(The "[line n]" marks show the line numbers printed in the margin of the original extract (lines 5, 10 and 15); the questions refer to lines 1, 4, 10 and 19 by the words they quote.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) In which month and year did a UN-supervised plebiscite *(line 1)* take place in Cameroon?

(ii) Write out the initials UNO *(line 4)* in full.

(iii) Which were the **two** plebiscite questions the UNO imposed on the people of British Cameroon *(line 4)*.

[2+1+2 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Month and year.** **February 1961**: the plebiscite was held on **11 February 1961** in both Southern and Northern Cameroons. (An earlier UN-supervised vote had been held in Northern Cameroons in November 1959, but it did not settle the question, so a second vote took place in 1961.) (2 marks)

**(ii) UNO.** **United Nations Organisation.** (1 mark)

**(iii) The two questions.** The voters had to say whether they wished:
1. to **achieve independence by joining the independent Federation of Nigeria**; or
2. to **achieve independence by joining the independent Republic of Cameroon** (then called Cameroun).

The UN rejected a third choice (independence on its own for Southern Cameroons). (2 marks: 1 for each question)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Name the leaders of (a) Republic of Cameroon and (b) Southern Cameroons *(line 10)* who met in Foumban.

(ii) Apart from those mentioned in the text, suggest **three** key provisions of the Foumban Conference.

[2+3 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The leaders.**
- (a) For the Republic of Cameroon: **President Ahmadou Ahidjo**.
- (b) For Southern Cameroons: **John Ngu Foncha**, the Prime Minister of Southern Cameroons and leader of the KNDP, who led the Southern Cameroons delegation (the opposition leader E. M. L. Endeley and other Southern Cameroons politicians were also in the delegation). (2 marks)

**(ii) Three key provisions (apart from the three governments, four Houses, common currency and the names and capitals of the two states in the text).** Any three of:
1. The country was to be a **Federal Republic of Cameroon** with **Yaounde as the federal capital**.
2. **French and English** were to be the two **official languages** of the Federation.
3. The **President** of the Federal Republic would be from East Cameroon and the **Vice-President** from West Cameroon (in practice Ahidjo and Foncha), and the President would appoint the Prime Ministers of the two states.
4. **Federal powers** such as defence, foreign affairs, nationality and currency were given to the federal government, with the other matters left to the federated states.
5. **Safeguard for West Cameroon:** a revision of the Constitution had to be passed by a majority that included the majority of the representatives of West Cameroon, and a revision that threatened the unity of the Federation was not meant to be admissible.
6. The **Federal Constitution** was to be the supreme law, and the legal and educational systems of the two states were left as they were (common law in West Cameroon, French civil law in East Cameroon).
(3 marks: 1 mark for each valid provision)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) Identify the **three** governments mentioned in the text that were set up in Foumban.

(ii) Give **two** reasons why Foumban was chosen as the venue for constitutional discussions.

[3+2 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The three governments.**
1. The **Federal Government** of the Federal Republic of Cameroon (seat at Yaounde);
2. The government of the Federated State of **East Cameroon** (Yaounde);
3. The government of the Federated State of **West Cameroon** (Buea).
(3 marks, 1 for each)

**(ii) Two reasons why Foumban was chosen.** Any two of:
1. Foumban, the capital of the Bamoum kingdom, lies in French Cameroun but **near the border with Southern Cameroons**, so it was within reach of the Southern Cameroons delegates from Bamenda and the Grassfields.
2. It was seen as a **neutral ground**, neither in the capital Yaounde of the Republic nor in Buea or Bamenda in Southern Cameroons.
3. It had **historical and cultural prestige** as the seat of the Bamoum Sultanate of King Njoya, who had invented the Bamoum script, and its traditional rulers shared a culture with the peoples of the Grassfields of Southern Cameroons, so the meeting symbolised reunification of peoples.
4. President Ahidjo, who was from the North, was on good terms with the Bamoum traditional authorities, so the meeting could be well hosted and peaceful (a reason given in some textbooks).
(2 marks, 1 for each reason)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) Identify **two** of the four Houses that were created in Foumban as mentioned in the text.

(ii) What important amendments *(line 19)* were later made of the constitution after 1972 that had long term consequences for the country?

[2+3 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Two of the four Houses.** Any two of:
1. The **Federal National Assembly** (the federal parliament, sitting at Yaounde);
2. The **West Cameroon House of Assembly** (the legislature of the state of West Cameroon);
3. The **West Cameroon House of Chiefs** (the second chamber of West Cameroon, made up of traditional rulers);
4. The **National Assembly (legislature) of East Cameroon**.
(2 marks, 1 for each)

**(ii) Important amendments after 1972 and their long term consequences.** Any three of:
1. **The 1972 constitution (20 May 1972).** Following a referendum in which voters were asked to approve a unitary state, the **federation was abolished** and the **United Republic of Cameroon** was created: one government, one National Assembly, and the two federated states were replaced by provinces (North West and South West provinces in the former West Cameroon).
   *Consequence:* the West Cameroon institutions (House of Assembly, House of Chiefs, Prime Minister) disappeared, which Anglophones felt as a loss of their autonomy and identity and which is still a source of complaint.
2. **Changes on the presidency (1975 and later).** The post of **Prime Minister** was created at national level in 1975 (the first holder was Paul Biya), and the Constitution was amended to make the Prime Minister the constitutional successor of the President.
   *Consequence:* this made possible the peaceful transfer of power to **Paul Biya** when President Ahidjo resigned in November 1982.
3. **Change of name (1984).** The United Republic of Cameroon was renamed the **Republic of Cameroon** (the name it had before reunification).
   *Consequence:* many Anglophones saw this as a sign that the union was ending and that the Francophone identity dominated.
4. **The 1996 Constitution (18 January 1996).** It introduced decentralisation with **Regions** and a **Senate**, recognised Cameroon as a decentralised unitary state and fixed the President's term in office; later amendments (for example in 2008) changed the term limits.
   *Consequence:* the creation of regions and the Senate was slow in being put into practice, and the debate on federalism and the Anglophone problem continues.
(3 marks: 1 mark for each valid amendment with a consequence)
